events.excerpt: Content This release reduces memory use and makes tx event searches cancellable. It addresses out-of-memory crashes on nodes serving GET /cosmos/tx/v1beta1/txs (and CometBFT RPC tx_search) for queries that match a very large number of transactions. This is a non-consensus release . The state machine is unchanged, so nodes can upgrade at any time with a rolling restart. No upgrade height or governance proposal is needed. Bug fixes Tx search loads only the requested page. Previously the kv indexer loaded every matching transaction into memory before taking out the requested page, even for limit=100. It now sorts and pages matches using the index keys and loads only the transactions on the requested page. In benchmarks with 100k matches, peak memory fell from 459 MB to 45 MB and latency from 474 ms to 95 ms. ( crypto-org-chain/cometbft#69 ) Tx searches stop when the client disconnects. GetTxsEvent and GetTx called CometBFT with a background context, so a search kept running after the client had timed out or disconnected. The request context is now passed through, and the search stops when the request is cancelled. ( crypto-org-chain/cosmos-sdk#1878 )

events.excerpt: [CONSTITUTIONAL] AIP: Update Arbitrum One and Nova L1-Pricing Parameters for Ethereum Glamsterdam Abstract This proposal updates the parentGasFloorPerToken and perBatchGasCharge parameters on Arbitrum One and Arbitrum Nova in response to Ethereum’s Glamsterdam upgrade. Glamsterdam changes the Ethereum gas costs associated with posting Arbitrum chain batches. Without corresponding parameter updates, the L1 fee paid by Arbitrum One and Nova users may no longer accurately reflect the cost of posting batches to Ethereum. The proposal authorizes targeted updates to the live parameters through the ArbOwner precompile. It does not introduce an ArbOS software upgrade or change the underlying L1-pricing algorithm. Motivation Arbitrum’s L1-pricing system estimates Ethereum gas cost of each batch, then uses that estimate to set the L1 fee paid by Arbitrum users and the amount the batch poster is paid back. Two parameters feed into this estimate: parentGasFloorPerToken , which mirrors Ethereum’s minimum gas charge for calldata; and perBatchGasCharge , which represents a fixed component of the estimated Ethereum gas cost attributed to each batch. The existing values reflect Ethereum’s pre-Glamsterdam cost structure. Following Glamsterdam’s activation, they may no longer accurately account for

events.excerpt: Since the DVP upgrade, ArbitrumDAO’s quorum is set as a share of delegated voting power: 50% for constitutional and 40% for non-constitutional proposals. This stopped token unlocks from pushing quorum up, but it moved the problem rather than solving it. Every delegated ARB that never votes now raises quorum without adding turnout, so incentives that reward delegation without checking whether that voting power is actually used can make quorum harder to reach. ABSTAIN votes count toward quorum and can carry thin proposals over the line, a large holder can delegate and stay silent to stall decisions, and lowering quorum again would make attacks cheaper. One possible answer is a neutral participation pool. The DAO funds it per epoch in advance, never per proposal, so nobody can buy turnout for their own vote. It pays only for votes actually cast: the same for FOR and AGAINST, less for ABSTAIN, with a cap per address. Rewards are computed from onchain VoteCast events and published as a Merkle root, so voters keep using Tally as usual. Delegates: is turnout still a real constraint after the DVP upgrade, and would a direction-neutral pool feel legitimate to you? In my free time I study consensus mechanisms and DAO governance. I’d build this as open source and may later apply for a grant
events.headline: Rewarding votes, not delegation: participation incentives under DVP quorum

events.excerpt: This release adds initial support for Fibre. Highlights Fibre client support: celestia-node now ships a built-in Fibre client, exposed under the new fibre JSON-RPC namespace on Light and Bridge nodes. Blobs are uploaded to Fibre Storage Providers and settled on-chain via an escrow-funded payment model — all driven locally by the node rather than routed through a bridge. The fibre namespace exposes: Submit — upload a blob and settle its MsgPayForFibre payment on-chain in one call. Upload — upload off-chain and settle the payment in the background. Download — retrieve a blob by its BlobID. Deposit / Withdraw — fund and unwind the escrow account that pays for storage. QueryEscrowAccount / PendingWithdrawals — inspect escrow balance and pending exits. Verified-header state client: DA nodes resolve validator sets and Fibre host addresses from the locally verified header chain (ABCI queries with Merkle-proof verification), so host discovery and payment validation don't rely on a trusted gRPC endpoint. [https://github.com/ /pull/5220 ] Requirements & notes Requires a configured core endpoint running celestia-app v10 (with the x/fibre and x/valaddr modules). Fibre is unavailable when no core endpoint is set. Breaking changes & upgrade notes Blob CLI input: blob submit now treats unprefix

The model points instead to the budget and to how profit is defined as the main levers. Below is what I propose, followed by the reasoning. The full report, model and data are linked at the end. What I propose Step 1. Now, through votes, no contract changes 1. Cut the Foundations budget for 2027 materially and, in the same vote, set the NEST threshold equal to the approved budget. I am asking for around $30M, about 30% below the current $43.8M. In the model, buybacks start to grow meaningfully from a cut of about 20% (roughly $35M), and a 30% cut roughly doubles them compared with today. The approved Foundations budget would serve as the operating baseline, not as a claim that it captures every DAO outflow; material off-budget spending, such as the $6.06M Kelp-related costs, would need to be reflected separately. 2. It encodes text, images, audio, and video, individually or combined in one input, into a shared 768-dimensional vector space for cross-modal retrieval, semantic similarity, clustering, and classification. events.excerpt: ℹ️ This is NOT a mandatory upgrade for validators. There is no coordinated halt or governance proposal. Nodes can upgrade whenever they like with a normal binary swap and restart. ⚙️ v6.6.4 is a small patch release on top of v6.6.3 🚀, aimed at operators running nodes in freeze mode 🧊 ( #3978 ). A frozen node halts one block below its freeze height and never processes another block. On v6.6.3 the EVM HTTP and WS servers only start after a block is processed, so a frozen node that restarted came back with its data and Tendermint RPC fine but its EVM RPC stuck offline 🔌. This release fixes that ( #4448 ). On startup a frozen node now initializes the app from its last block header, which starts the EVM servers just as processing a block would ✅. 🎯 Who Should Upgrade 🧊 Frozen historical RPC operators Strongly recommended : EVM RPC comes back after a restart 🖥️ RPC / full-node operators Optional: nodes not in freeze mode behave exactly as before 🛡️ Validators Optional: no state-machine or consensus-breaking changes ⏱️ Downtime Just a node restart; no coordinated halt What's Changed Initialize app from last header on frozen restart for v6.6 by @masih in #4448 Full Changelog : v6.6.3...v6.6.4 Experimental Pre-built Binaries Pre-built statically-linked seid binary attached below for linux

events.excerpt: Building Trisara (Colosseum hackathon): session-aware pricing infra for RWA markets: a real clock for equity prices onchain. The BONER/HIMS case is the exhibit: one meme cornered ~42% of HIMS on-chain float and pushed the wrapped token to $132 against a $28 real close over a weekend with the NYSE closed. No arb window fast enough to hold the two together. Uniswap routes >99% of tracked stock-token DeFi deposits on Robinhood Chain, so this lands on your pools first. I verified the root cause live (Chainlink equity feeds frozen 37.7h over weekends). Trisara’s PoolTwapAdapter + GuardedSwapRouter collars flow when the reference market is closed: a plug-in, not a fork. Is session-aware pricing something v4 hooks on RH Chain should standardize? Keen for the community’s take. 8 posts - 3 participants Read full topic
events.headline: [Discussion] Should v4 hooks on Robinhood Chain standardize session-aware pricing?

events.excerpt: Removal of the Wormhole adapter from a.DI governance forwarding to BNB Chain and threshold change from 3/4 to 2/3 Summary This proposal suggests removing the Wormhole adapter from Lido DAO governance forwarding to BNB Chain and lowering the required confirmations on BNB Chain from 3 of 4 to 2 of 3 bridges. Wormhole shut down automatic delivery for its Standard Relayer on 1 April 2026. The Lido Wormhole adapter depends on that relayer, so only Chainlink CCIP, LayerZero and Hyperlane can still deliver Lido DAO messages to BNB Chain. With three working bridges and a threshold of three, an outage or delay of any one of them blocks Lido DAO decisions on BNB Chain. A 2-of-3 threshold restores tolerance to one bridge outage; forging a message would then require compromising two bridges instead of three. Background Lido DAO decisions reach BNB Chain through a.DI , the cross-chain messaging layer built by BGD Labs and adopted for Lido under LIP-24 . The Lido DAO Agent sends a message to the CrossChainController on Ethereum , which forwards it through four bridges. The CrossChainController on BNB Chain accepts the message once 3 of the 4 bridges have delivered it. The CrossChainExecutor then executes it. Bridge Ethereum adapter BNB Chain adapter Chainlink CCIP 0x29D4fA5FCC282ba2788A2818607
events.headline: Reconfigure BSC governance forwarding after Wormhole auto delivery shutdown
